idiom_name: hand-written packed struct plus explicit encode/decode against the published schema
implementation_notes: C has neither reflection nor serialisation in its standard library, so the published language is realised by hand: one struct per schema message plus explicit pack/unpack functions that encode field order, widths and endianness, checked against a written schema document. Codegen removes most of that work when the contract is IDL-first - protoc --c_out with protobuf-c generates Foo__Bar structs with foo__bar__pack()/foo__bar__unpack() and descriptor tables, nanopb generates small pb_encode()/pb_decode() pairs from the same .proto for constrained targets - and CBOR (RFC 8949) is the self-describing binary option when a text format is too heavy. The hand-written form stays justified for fixed-layout legacy protocols, ABI-stable wire structs and builds that must not grow a toolchain.
pitfalls: Struct padding, alignment and integer widths are compiler- and ABI-dependent: dumping a struct with memcpy publishes a layout nobody else can read - serialise field by field with fixed widths and explicit byte order (htobe32/be32toh).
Fixed char arrays truncate silently and an unterminated wire string makes %s read past the buffer: bound every copy with the schema length and validate it before use.
Without generated code the schema survives only in comments: hand-written C structs must be covered by a conformance suite replaying published fixtures, or producers drift undetected.
